title: What Is Manual Warewashing?
excerpt: Manual warewashing is the controlled hand-cleaning process for utensils and equipment: preclean, wash, rinse, sanitize where required, then air-dry and store without recontamination.
content_html:
Manual warewashing is the hand-operated process used to clean utensils and equipment when an approved mechanical warewashing machine is not being used. Its purpose is not simply to make items look clean; the process controls food soil, cleaning chemicals and microorganisms before items return to food use.

The common model-code sequence

The 2026 FDA Food Code uses a three-stage manual warewashing framework—washing, rinsing and sanitizing—with precleaning before washing and protected drying/storage afterward. Many jurisdictions use similar principles, but facilities must follow their own adopted food code.

1. Preclean

Scrape, drain or otherwise remove food debris that would overload the wash solution. Heavily soiled items may need appropriate presoaking or additional precleaning so detergent can reach the surface.

2. Wash

Wash with the approved cleaning agent and the mechanical action needed to loosen and remove soil. The method should match the utensil or equipment and the type of soil.

3. Rinse

Rinsing removes loosened food debris, abrasive material and cleaning chemicals before sanitizing. A dirty or detergent-loaded rinse step can undermine the process.

4. Sanitize where required

After cleaning and rinsing, food-contact surfaces and utensils are sanitized using the approved method and parameters required by the applicable food code and sanitizer or equipment instructions. Use the required measuring or test device; do not estimate sanitizer control by smell or colour.

5. Air-dry

Allow cleaned and sanitized items to air-dry as required by the applicable procedure. Towel-drying can recontaminate a clean utensil if the towel is not controlled for that purpose.

6. Protect during storage

Store clean items where splash, dust, hands, waste or dirty equipment cannot recontaminate them. Wet nesting or stacking can also prevent proper drying.

About three-compartment sinks

The FDA Food Code model generally provides for at least three sink compartments for manual washing, rinsing and sanitizing, with approved alternatives for special constraints. This is a model-code reference; local rules determine what a specific facility must provide.

Common manual-warewashing failures

  • Skipping scraping or precleaning.
  • Using dirty wash or rinse solution.
  • Overloading sink compartments.
  • Incorrect sanitizer setup or no verification.
  • Mixing clean and dirty items.
  • Towel-drying or stacking items before they are properly dry.

Practical takeaway

Manual warewashing is a controlled sequence: preclean → wash → rinse → sanitize as required → air-dry → protected storage. Each step depends on the previous one being completed correctly.

References

  1. U.S. FDA — FDA Food Code 2026, Chapter 4.
  2. U.S. FDA — Food Code 2026.
  3. FAO/WHO Codex — General Principles of Food Hygiene.
